title: How Bollywood's Casting Directors Went From Sidelines to Creative Powerhouses
excerpt: Forbes India's Showstoppers 2026 edition spotlights the rise of casting directors as creative collaborators who are reshaping Indian cinema by championing fresh talent over star power.
body:
• Forbes India's Showstoppers 2026 edition recognises casting directors as key creative collaborators who have transformed how Bollywood discovers and uses talent.
  • Casting director Mukesh Chhabra, whose credits span from Gangs of Wasseypur to Jawan, says every major filmmaker now works with casting directors — a shift from a decade ago when few took the role seriously.
  • Self-tapes and remote auditions have democratised access, enabling actors from Kashmir to Chennai to audition without relocating to Mumbai.
  • Chhabra and choreographer Bosco Martis recently launched The Big Break, a digital-first talent hunt for actors, singers and dancers.

For decades, casting in Bollywood was an afterthought — a process driven by star power, nepotism and the producer's bottom line. That is changing. Forbes India's annual Showstoppers 2026 edition, which ranks India's 100 biggest celebrities, has highlighted a quiet revolution: the casting director has moved from behind the scenes to become a creative collaborator who shapes the films audiences see.

Breaking the Typecast

The scale of the shift is striking. Actor Jagdish Raj Khurana once held a Guinness World Record for playing a police inspector in 144 Hindi films. That kind of typecasting defined an era. Today, casting directors are the disruptors breaking that mould.

https://x.com/ForbesIndia/status/2097198298264392011

“When I began, casting directors weren't taken seriously by most filmmakers,” said Mukesh Chhabra, founder of Mukesh Chhabra Casting Company, whose credits include Dangal, Sanju, Jawan and Dunki, in an interview with Hollywood Reporter India. “Only visionaries like Anurag Kashyap and Vishal Bhardwaj, who knew us from Delhi theatre days, recognised our contributions.”

That landscape has transformed entirely. “Today, every filmmaker, whether it's Anees Bazmee, David Dhawan, or even directors from the '90s, works with casting directors,” Chhabra said.

Casting Coups That Changed Films

Romil Modi orchestrated two of 2024's most celebrated casting decisions. For Laapataa Ladies, he introduced debutants Pratibha Ranta, Nitanshi Goel and Sparsh Shrivastava, whose raw performances became the film's defining feature. For All We Imagine as Light, he assembled an ensemble led by Kani Kusruti and Divya Prabha that helped the film earn international acclaim.

“Casting isn't just about matching talent to roles; it's about creating the foundation for a film. If the casting is right, 80 per cent of the film's work is done.”

— Romil Modi, Casting Director

Tess Joseph, who cast The White Tiger and Lion, described the shift from a different angle. “We're changing the game by finding diamonds in the rough,” she told Hollywood Reporter India. “The growth of artists who have no backing is a result of filmmakers trusting casting directors to champion talent. We're often the first to see potential, and we fight for it.”

Technology Opens the Door

The pandemic accelerated a trend that was already underway. Self-tapes and remote auditions have removed geographic barriers, enabling actors from small towns across India to compete for roles they would never have accessed before.

“With India's diverse talent pool, we're casting actors from all across the country — Kashmir, Chennai, Vishakhapatnam, Manali, Chandigarh — and even internationally,” said casting director Paragg Mehta, whose credits include Gadar 2. He recalled pushing for Vikrant Massey during auditions for Lipstick Under My Burkha in 2016, despite initial resistance from the director — a bet that paid off as Massey went on to deliver a career-defining performance in 12th Fail.

What's Next

Chhabra and choreographer Bosco Martis are now betting that the same democratisation can extend beyond the audition room. In August 2026, they launched The Big Break, a digital-first talent hunt for actors, singers and dancers, according to Bollywood Hungama. The platform aims to bring the audition process directly to performers across the country, with selected participants advancing to Mumbai for competition rounds under industry mentors.

As actor Ali Fazal put it at a recent roundtable: “Casting directors are changing the game.” The Forbes India Showstoppers edition suggests the industry is finally catching on.
